claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated creep.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order enhance diffusion at the layer interfaces.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order promote dislocation climb at the layer interfaces.
The starting coatings have distinct nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers with compositional complexity and lattice distortion.
Nanoscale interfaces between the high-entropy-alloy layers mediate the creep response.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion promote differences in short-range order at the interfaces.
Intrinsic lattice distortion and short-range order induce stress concentrations at the interfaces during sustained loading.
Interfacial stress concentrations accelerate diffusion-assisted dislocation climb.
Interfacial stress concentrations accelerate local interface sliding.
Slower loading rates provide more time for diffusion-based deformation processes to operate.
Lower loading rates will produce greater strain accumulation than faster loading rates.
Lower loading rates will produce more observable evidence of interfacial sliding and dislocation climb than faster loading rates.
The creep rate will be higher under slow loading than under fast loading.
Faster loading leaves less time for diffusion and interface-mediated processes and therefore reduces progressive plastic deformation.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the nanoscale layered morphology remains intact and delamination or complete interface failure does not occur.
The proposed mechanism is limited to conditions that do not induce phase transformation or other degradation modes.
Conventional dislocation glide may compete with the proposed diffusion-assisted mechanism in some loading regimes.
Failure of reduced loading rate to increase interfacial climb, diffusion indicators, or creep response would falsify the proposed rate-dependent interface-mediated mechanism.
